Faults of speech are extremely grave offenses, for they injure the harmony between Heaven and Earth and offend against what the gods hold taboo, and are equal in weight to the offenses of killing and of licentiousness. Mr. Zhao Kangjing of the Song dynasty once trained his mind each day with a bottle and white and black beans. Whenever a good thought arose, he dropped a white bean into the bottle; whenever an evil thought arose, he dropped in a black bean. In the evening he poured the beans out and counted them, recording his good and evil. When he first began, the black beans he put in were very many; later they gradually grew fewer. In time he forgot even the two kinds of thought, good and evil, and entered the state of “no thought of good, no thought of evil,” a mind without a single stray thought; at the last he even threw away the bottle and the beans and had no more use for them.

Every stirring of our minds, every word and deed, every way we treat others and receive things, are watched and recorded by the gods at all times and in all places; do not let your evil thoughts continue without pause. If by chance an evil thought arises, you must at once become aware of it and turn it around. Therefore in mastering oneself one must begin by mastering where mastery is hardest, and probe all the way to the place where thoughts arise and cease. If one can work in this way, then our boundless karmic obstructions can in a single moment become pure and clear, like empty space. And if one can do this, then the power to grant or take away good and ill fortune, long life or short, lies in our own hands.

Therefore, before the image of the Great Being Avalokiteshvara enshrined in his family hall, Lord Yu knocked his head until it bled and reverently made this vow: “May my good thoughts be forever pure, and my power of good advance vigorously; if I give myself the slightest indulgence in cutting off evil and practicing good, may I fall forever into hell.” Every morning at dawn he devoutly recited the holy name of the Great Compassionate and Great Merciful One a hundred times, praying for the Bodhisattva’s protection. blocks.text: 1. Bitterly Suffering the Punishment of Heaven

inline.s: In the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty, Lord Yu of Jiangxi, whose personal name was Du and whose courtesy name was Liangchen, was richly talented and widely learned. At eighteen he passed the county examination as a xiucai, and in every examination of the county school he always ranked at the head.

When he reached manhood, his family was poor, and he made his living by teaching. With more than ten fellow students of the county school he formed the Wenchang Society, honoring the instruction of Emperor Lord Wenchang: cherishing the written word, releasing living creatures, abstaining from licentiousness, abstaining from killing, and abstaining from faults of speech — practicing in this way for many years.

Yet he sat for the examination seven times, one after another, and passed none. He had five sons, four of whom died of illness in childhood. Only the third remained, exceedingly clever and handsome, with a pair of moles on the sole of his left foot; the husband and wife treasured him as a jewel, but at eight years old, while at play in the neighborhood, he was lost. He had four daughters, of whom only one was raised. Because of the children who died young and the beloved son who was lost, his wife wept until both her eyes went blind. Lord Yu remained poor and dejected the whole year through, and his straits grew worse and worse.

blocks.text: 2. Was There Then No Great Fault?

inline.s: Reflecting on himself, Lord Yu found that he had no great fault, and yet he bitterly suffered the punishment of Heaven. From past the age of forty, at the end of every year he would use yellow paper to write out a petition and pray to the Stove God, entreating him to report on high to the Jade Emperor the matter of his having no great fault and yet bitterly suffering the punishment of Heaven. In this way he did for several years, and still there was no response.

In his forty-seventh year, on New Year’s Eve, Lord Yu sat through the night with his blind wife and their one daughter. The whole house was cold and bare, and they faced one another in desolation, sad beyond bearing. Suddenly he heard a knock at the door, and Lord Yu took up a candle to look. He beheld a gentleman in a black robe and a scholar’s cap, his beard and hair half grey, who made a deep bow and took a seat. He announced himself, saying, “My surname is Zhang. I have just returned from a long journey, and hearing your mournful sighs, I have come especially to comfort you.” Lord Yu was astonished in his heart at the coming of this man, and treated him with the greatest reverence. He therefore told him of himself: that all his life he had studied widely and accumulated many good deeds, and yet for thirty years he had sat for the juren examination and to this day had not passed; that of his children some had died and some were lost, and his wife’s eyes had wept themselves blind; that the whole family could barely keep itself in food and clothing; and he read aloud to Zhang the petitions he had burned in prayer to the Stove God.

blocks.text: 3. The Mind of Evil Stirring Without Rest

inline.s: Zhang said, “I have known what happens in your home for a long time. Your mind of evil is far too heavy; you devote yourself wholly to empty reputation, and your petition is full of resentment and indignation, irreverently laid before the Lord on High. I fear the punishment you are to receive will not stop here.”

Lord Yu was greatly alarmed and said, “I have heard that in the unseen realm even the smallest good deed is surely recorded. I have sworn to practice good deeds and have reverently and scrupulously observed the rules of the Wenchang Society for many years — can it all be empty reputation?”

Zhang said, “The truth of the matter is not as you say. Take, for instance, the article on cherishing the written word among the rules you observe: your pupils and friends often use pages of books, essays, and old volumes to paper windows and wrap parcels, and even to wipe tables, and then, on the pretext of not defiling them, burn them straightway. You see this with your own eyes day after day and never utter a single word of warning; you merely pick up written paper you find in the street, carry it home, and consign it to the fire. What benefit is there in that?

When the society releases living creatures each month, you do no more than bustle along with the crowd and drift with the current. If no one else takes the initiative, you simply let it be; in truth, no thought of compassion has ever arisen from within you.

Moreover, in your own household, shrimps and crabs and the like are also brought to the kitchen and cooked and eaten. You say you abstain from killing living creatures — are they alone not living beings?

And as for the fault of speech: your words are quick and subtle, and those who hear you are often filled with admiration. When you speak, you know in your own heart that you are wounding kindness, yet when you talk of persons or affairs with familiar friends, you always ridicule and mock and sting, and cannot restrain yourself. Your tongue is like a sharp knife: light, unkind, and slanderous, and wherever its edge reaches it angers gods and spirits. The underworld long ago recorded these evil deeds of yours in its ledgers, and there is no telling how many there are — and still you set yourself up as simple and generous. Question your own heart: whom are you trying to deceive? Would you deceive Heaven?

Again, as for abstaining from lust: though you have committed no actual deed of sexual misconduct, whenever you see another man’s beautiful daughter you must gaze at her long and steadily, and your mind sways and cannot still itself. It is only that no illicit occasion has come together for you. Turn and examine yourself: if she came knocking at your door in the night, could you be like the chaste man of Lu, who shut his door and would not admit her? Yet you declare that in all your life you have had no improper desire, and that you can face Heaven, Earth, and the gods and spirits. This is truly absurd in the extreme!
These are the very rules you vowed to keep strictly, and you have not truly kept a single one of them — to say nothing of the rest.

The petitions you have burned year after year have all been laid before Heaven. The Jade Emperor commanded the Messenger Who Travels by Day to observe your good and evil for several years, yet not one good deed was to be recorded. He saw only that when you were privately alone, thoughts of greed, thoughts of lust, thoughts of envy, thoughts of narrow impatience, thoughts of exalting yourself and belittling others, thoughts of recalling the past and anticipating the future, thoughts of hoping others would repay your kindness, and thoughts of taking revenge for wrongs done to you came and went in your breast with no end at all. These manifold evils of the mind are firmly knotted within you; the gods have recorded them in abundance, and Heaven’s punishment will grow daily heavier. You will have no leisure even to flee disaster — by what right could you still seek blessings from Heaven?

Lord Yu was astonished and afraid; he knelt on the ground with tears streaming down his face and said, “Since you, sir, understand the affairs of the unseen, you must be a venerable deity. I beg you to save me and point out a road to life.”

Zhang said, “You are a man of learning who understands propriety, and you also know the joy of admiring what is good. When you hear a good word, you are stirred to exhortation; when you see a good deed, you are inspired beyond measure. But no sooner has it passed than you forget it. This is because the root of your faith was never deep, and so your virtue cannot endure. Hence the good words and good deeds of your whole life have been mere perfunctory drifting; when was even one thing done in earnest? Moreover, with your breast full of evil intent, rising and falling, winding on and on, you still would demand fine rewards from Heaven — like planting thorns over all the ground and foolishly hoping to harvest fine grain. Is that not a great mistake?

From this day forward, whenever thoughts of greed, of lust, of violence, or of delusion and other stray thoughts arise, first summon fierce resolve and sweep them all away, clearing them out utterly, so that a single thought attends only to the side of good. If there is a good deed within your power to perform, seek no reward and no fame; whether great or small, hard or easy, do it solidly and steadily, with patience. If it lies beyond your power, then be diligent and earnest all the same, so that this good intention may be perfected. First, have the mind of patience; second, have the mind of perseverance. Never indulge your own sloth; never deceive yourself. Practice thus long and long, and you will surely reap effects beyond all reckoning.

“Your family has served me with great reverence and purity, and so I have come especially to tell you these things. You must quickly do your utmost to carry them out, and only then can you turn back the will of Heaven.” When he had finished speaking, Zhang walked into the inner chamber. Lord Yu rose and followed him, and when they reached the stove he suddenly vanished. Only then did he understand that this was the Stove God, and so he burned incense and bowed in thanks.

blocks.text: 6. Storing Blessing to Turn Heaven’s Mind

inline.s: In the year Lord Yu was fifty — the second year of the Wanli reign — the metropolitan examination was held, and juren from every region came to the capital to sit for the jinshi examination. At that time Zhang Jiangling was first grand secretary (the equivalent of a chancellor), presiding over the great affairs of the Grand Secretariat. After the metropolitan examination closed he went to visit his fellow provincials from Jiangxi who had come to the capital for it, wishing to choose a teacher of both sound character and learning for his son. Everyone with one voice recommended Lord Yu. And so Zhang Jiangling engaged him to come to the capital as a family tutor, and Lord Yu brought his family with him.

Zhang Jiangling held Lord Yu’s moral cultivation in high esteem, and, citing existing precedent, approved his admission to study at the Imperial College. In the fourth year of Wanli, Lord Yu sat the provincial examination in the capital and passed as a juren, and the following year he passed as a jinshi.

One day Lord Yu went to call on the eunuch Lord Yang. Lord Yang had long heard of Lord Yu’s virtue and learning, and had his five sons come out to bow to him. They were all children he had sought and bought from every region, to be his heirs and cheer his old age. One of them was sixteen, and Lord Yu found his features very familiar, and asked him where he was from. He answered, “I am a man of Jiangxi. In childhood I mistakenly boarded a grain boat and was carried away from my home district; even now I vaguely remember my original surname and the look of my neighborhood.” And so he told it all in detail. When Lord Yu had heard him out he was greatly astonished, and had him take off the shoe and sock of his left foot; he saw the pair of moles on the sole of his foot, still as in childhood. Lord Yu cried out aloud, “You are my son!”

Lord Yang was astonished as well, and at once sent the boy home with Lord Yu to his lodging. Lord Yu hurried to tell his wife. She felt over her son and wept bitterly, tears of blood bursting forth. The boy too wept without ceasing, and holding his mother’s face in both hands, he licked her blind eyes with his tongue, and his mother’s two eyes suddenly saw the light again.

Grief and joy mingled in Lord Yu’s heart. He had no wish for office; he took leave of Zhang Jiangling and returned to his native place. Zhang Jiangling greatly admired this true and sincere devotion, and gave him generous gifts to speed him on his way. When Lord Yu returned to his native place he devoted himself to good all the more. After his son took a wife, seven sons were born in succession and all were raised; they were all able to carry on the family’s tradition of learning.

Lord Yu wrote down with his own hand the story of his meeting the Stove God and of truly reforming his faults, in order to instruct his sons and grandsons. He enjoyed health and long life, living to the age of eighty-eight and passing away without illness. People all said that this was the reward of truly practicing good deeds and turning back the will of Heaven.
Recorded by Luo Zhen, a later student of the same neighborhood.
